name: Oral squamous cell carcinoma
aliases: squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity

clinicalPearls: Oral squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the oral cavity and often presents as a non-healing ulcer, lump, or persistent red or white patch
Classic worrying features are an indurated ulcer with rolled margins, fixation to underlying tissue, and failure to heal beyond two to three weeks
Tobacco in all forms, areca nut, and alcohol are the dominant risk factors and act synergistically
The lateral and ventral tongue and the floor of mouth are high-risk sites, though any oral surface can be affected
Early lesions may be painless, so any persistent oral abnormality warrants a high index of suspicion and referral
Cervical lymphadenopathy, especially firm or fixed nodes, may indicate regional metastatic spread
Definitive diagnosis requires biopsy, and staging guides treatment involving surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy as appropriate
Prognosis depends heavily on stage at diagnosis, underscoring the value of early detection and opportunistic screening
reference.pathophysiology: Oral squamous cell carcinoma develops through the accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations in oral keratinocytes, typically driven by chronic exposure to carcinogens such as tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol. Many tumours arise within or adjacent to potentially malignant disorders such as leukoplakia or erythroplakia, progressing through increasing grades of epithelial dysplasia to carcinoma in situ and then invasive disease when malignant cells breach the basement membrane. The invasive tumour infiltrates local tissue, can destroy bone, and spreads via lymphatics to cervical nodes, with distant metastasis in advanced disease. Field change means the whole mucosa is at risk of further primaries.
additionalDifferentials: Oral leukoplakia or erythroplakia without invasion
Chronic infective ulcers such as tuberculosis or syphilis
Salivary gland or other oral malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Incisional biopsy of the lesion for histological diagnosis and grading
Examination and imaging of the neck for lymph node involvement
Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI) to assess local extent and staging
Assessment for distant metastasis and synchronous primaries
redFlags: Any oral ulcer or lesion persisting beyond two to three weeks requires urgent specialist referral to exclude cancer
Induration, fixation, rolled margins, or spontaneous bleeding of a lesion
Unexplained firm or fixed cervical lymphadenopathy
Persistent unexplained pain, numbness, loosening of teeth, or difficulty swallowing
reference.prognosis: Outcome is strongly stage-dependent, with early localised disease carrying a favourable prognosis, whereas advanced tumours with nodal involvement have substantially poorer survival and higher morbidity from treatment.
pitfalls: Attributing a persistent ulcer to trauma or denture irritation and delaying biopsy
Reassurance because a lesion is painless, since early cancers are often symptomless
Failing to examine and palpate the neck for nodal disease
Overlooking the risk of second primaries in a field-changed mucosa
